strengths: Novel and clearly motivated problem: reconstructing sharp, animatable 3DGS human avatars from motion-blurred multi-view video is an unaddressed task, and the paper convincingly explains why blur hurts existing avatar methods (distorted 3DGS representation and erroneous SMPL estimation).

Well-founded technical approach: the 3D-aware blur formation model (Eq. 7-9) physically extends the 2D blur integration into the SMPL-driven canonical 3DGS pipeline, and the B-Spline sub-frame pose parameterization plus non-rigid displacement is a sensible decomposition of the ill-posed deblurring problem. The inter-frame continuity regularization (Eq. 15) directly targets the directional ambiguity illustrated in Fig. 1, and Table 6 shows it mainly fixes non-middle timesteps, supporting the claim.

Strong benchmark contribution: a synthetic dataset built from ZJU-MoCap (with RIFE-interpolated averaging for realistic blur) and a genuinely new real-captured dataset using a 12-camera 360-degree hybrid-exposure system with ND filters to equalize brightness - a careful and well-documented acquisition setup (Table 1). Public release of code and data adds reproducibility value.

Substantial and consistent quantitative gains: ~2.4-2.5 dB PSNR over all two-stage baselines on both datasets (Tables 2-3), robust across blur magnitudes K=5,7,9,11 (Table 8), and the paper gives a plausible explanation for why 2D-deblur+3DGS baselines saturate (cross-view inconsistency).

Thorough ablations: individual components (interpolation, non-rigid displacement, LBS optimization, shape optimization), sensitivity to control knots P and virtual image count T, and the L_reg study - all with both quantitative and qualitative evidence, plus an honest limitations discussion (foreground-background blending, mask dependence).
weaknesses: Limited baseline breadth: the only avatar backbone compared is GauHuman, and the only baselines are two-stage 2D deblurring pipelines. The claim that multi-view deblurring methods [26,39,63,76] are inapplicable is asserted rather than empirically demonstrated; a brief adaptation attempt (e.g., Bad-Gaussians with per-frame camera) would strengthen the comparison. There is also no comparison against pose-refinement variants (e.g., GauHuman with the correction module mentioned in footnote 1), leaving the benefit of the 3D-aware motion model vs. simpler pose refinement partially untested.

Evaluation protocol has caveats: SMPL parameters are calibrated with EasyMoCap on the blurry videos, and masks come from Segment-Anything; both propagate potential errors into all methods, and the paper does not quantify how sensitive the results are to SMPL initialization quality on blurry input - a key aspect of the claimed second failure mode of blur.

Benchmark scale is modest: six subjects on the synthetic side and only eight scenes for the real dataset, with a single-seed reporting of metrics and no variance/uncertainty estimates. The reported gains are large enough that this is unlikely to overturn conclusions, but statistical robustness is unverified.

Some redundancy and polish issues: Section 2.1 repeats nearly identical paragraphs about the deblurring paradigm; typos such as 'SMLP model' (Sec. 3.2 end), 'datset', 'differnet', and 'harness' (should be 'hamper') in Sec. 5.5 slightly hurt clarity. Key implementation details (weights of L_reg, number of Gaussians, training time) are deferred or omitted from the main text.

The blur synthesis on the synthetic dataset uses RIFE-interpolated averaging of K=5 frames, which produces relatively smooth blur; evaluation is on sharp novel views of the 18 remaining cameras, so the metrics measure novel-view sharpness rather than direct deblurring quality, which is a reasonable but non-obvious choice that could be better justified.
No analysis of training/rendering cost relative to GauHuman despite rendering T virtual images per blurry frame per camera; practical runtime impact is unknown.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely new problem — reconstructing sharp, animatable 3DGS human avatars from motion-blurred multi-view video — and the framing of blur formation in 3D canonical space (averaging rendered sub-frame images via SMPL-parameterized warping, Eq. 9) is physically sensible and well-motivated by the ambiguity analysis in Fig. 1.

The benchmark contribution is substantial: a synthetic blurred dataset built from ZJU-MoCap (six subjects, RIFE-interpolated averaging to reduce discontinuities) and a real dataset captured with a purpose-built 360-degree hybrid-exposure system (blurry/sharp cameras synchronized, exposure ratio 16x with ND filter for intensity consistency). Very few submissions construct real hardware for a new task.

The evaluation is reasonably thorough: comparisons against four two-stage 2D-deblurring + GauHuman pipelines, ablations of all major components (interpolation, non-rigid displacement, LBS optimization, shape optimization), sensitivity analyses of control knots P, virtual image count T, and blur magnitude Kblur (Tabs. 6–9), plus the inter-frame regularization loss Lreg ablated specifically at non-middle timesteps (Tab. 6, Fig. 7), which directly tests the claimed directional-ambiguity fix.
Reported gains are consistent and sizable (e.g., PSNR 25.55 vs. ~23.08 for all baselines on synthetic; LPIPS 0.1476 vs. ~0.22), and hold across blur magnitudes Kblur = 5–11.
Limitations are honestly discussed (background/foreground blending not modeled, dependence on pre-computed masks, Fig. 8), and code/data are stated to be released, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The baseline comparison is narrow. All quantitative comparisons are against GauHuman, directly or behind four 2D deblurbers. The related-work section cites dynamic-scene deblurring NeRF/3DGS methods ([2, 57, 60]) that are dismissed as 'inapplicable,' but with multi-view SMPL initialization available, adapting at least one such method or a stronger avatar baseline (e.g., GaussianAvatar [10], 3DGS-Avatar [52]) would substantially strengthen the claim of superiority. As written, the gap could partly reflect GauHuman's weaknesses rather than the blur modeling.

The synthetic blur model may not faithfully represent real motion blur: averaging RIFE-interpolated frames of 15 FPS captures produces smooth, temporally coherent blur, whereas real 50 ms exposures of fast human motion contain non-linear trajectories and rolling-shutter effects. The claimed sim-to-real transfer is supported only by the real dataset's own baselines, which share the same EasyMoCal-calibrated SMPL init; no cross-validation (e.g., evaluating the synthetic-trained recipe on real data qualitatively) is provided.

The real dataset evaluation is weak: only 8 scenes, PSNR/SSIM computed against sharp novel-view frames while training uses only 4 blurry views — this confounds deblurring quality with view-count effects. There is no evaluation of motion/pose accuracy (e.g., sub-frame motion recovery is a core claim but is never quantitatively measured against any ground-truth trajectory), and no user study or perceptual assessment despite deblurring being partly a perceptual task.

Some quantitative evidence is underwhelming relative to the framing: on the real dataset the two-stage baselines (e.g., 25.57 PSNR) already nearly match direct GauHuman (25.60), and the ablation deltas are small (full model 27.01 vs. 26.96 w/o shape opt., 26.82 w/o LBS opt. in Tab. 4), suggesting some components contribute marginally; no variance/error bars are reported for any result.

Writing and presentation issues are material enough to note: the Related Work contains a nearly verbatim duplicated paragraph (end of Sec. 2.1 is repeated at the top of p.3); there are recurring typos ('SMLP' for SMPL, 'datset', 'differnet', 'harness' used where 'hinder' is meant); Eq. 7-8's normalization factor φ is introduced then dropped; and key implementation details (training iterations, runtime, number of Gaussians, how T relates to Kblur at training vs. test time) are deferred or absent, which hampers reproducibility despite the code release promise.

The method largely assembles existing pieces (SMPL-based canonical 3DGS from GauHuman, B-spline pose interpolation, sub-frame exposure averaging as in BAD-NeRF/BAD-Gaussians) with the novelty concentrated in applying bundle-adjusted deblurring to articulated humans. This is a legitimate contribution, but the paper should be more precise about which elements are new versus transferred.

strengths: Novel problem formulation: the paper is plausibly the first to tackle reconstruction of sharp, animatable 3DGS human avatars directly from motion-blurred multi-view RGB video, filling a genuine gap between 2D video deblurring and 3D human avatar modeling.

Technically sound core idea: extending the 2D blur formation model (Eq. 7-8) into a 3D-aware formulation (Eq. 9) that averages virtual sharp renderings warped by interpolated SMPL parameters is well-motivated and cleanly decomposes the ill-posed problem into sub-frame motion estimation plus canonical avatar reconstruction.

Thoughtful motion modeling: B-spline pose interpolation over the exposure window, a learned non-rigid pose displacement, an inter-frame continuity regularization (L_reg) to resolve motion-direction ambiguity, and LBS/shape refinement are all reasonable components, each validated in ablations (Tab. 4, 5, 6, 7).

Strong empirical evidence: consistent gains over a GauHuman-based baseline and four two-stage deblur-then-reconstruct pipelines on both synthetic (+~2.5 dB PSNR, large LPIPS improvement) and real captured data, with ablations under multiple blur magnitudes (K_blur = 5,7,9,11) demonstrating robustness.

Valuable benchmark contribution: a synthetic dataset derived from ZJU-MoCap with RIFE-interpolated blur synthesis, and especially a real dataset captured with a purpose-built 360-degree hybrid-exposure camera rig (long-exposure blurry views + synchronized short-exposure sharp views with ND-filtered intensity matching), which is a significant data-collection effort for a new task.
Honest limitations section: the authors clearly identify the unmodeled foreground-background blending and the dependence on pre-computed masks, supported by a qualitative failure case (Fig. 8).
The stated intent to release code and dataset supports reproducibility of a new benchmark.
weaknesses: Baseline coverage is somewhat narrow. The main comparison is GauHuman trained on blurry frames and 2D deblurring + GauHuman pipelines. The authors dismiss deblurring NeRF/3DGS methods (BAD-NeRF, BAD-Gaussians, DP-NeRF, Deblur-NeRF) as restricted to camera motion/defocus; while largely accurate, a discussion or an adapted variant (e.g., bundle-adjusting a rigid human root trajectory within such a framework) would strengthen the claim that no comparable 3D-aware baseline exists.

Some ablated components yield small gains (e.g., 'w/o shape opt.' differs from the full model by ~0.05 dB PSNR on both datasets; 'w/o LBS opt.' by ~0.2 dB), and the gains of full model over its strongest ablation are within a narrow margin; the contribution of individual modules is modest even if the overall system gain is clear.

Synthetic blur generation (averaging 5 RIFE-interpolated frames) is an approximation of true long-exposure blur and may not capture realistic exposure-time intensity integration; the real dataset mitigates but does not eliminate this concern, and ground-truth sharp frames for the training views are unavailable in the real setting (only novel-view sharp evaluation).

The method assumes static cameras, per-sequence shared shape, and pre-computed SMPL fits/masks from blurry inputs; error propagation from EasyMoCap SMPL estimation on blurry frames is not quantified, and the effect of mask quality is not ablated.

Practical costs are unreported: no training time, memory footprint, or optimization iterations are given, and 50 blurry frames per camera is a small training set, raising questions about scalability to longer sequences.

Presentation issues: duplicated paragraph in Related Work (Sec. 2.1 repeats nearly identical text across pages 2-3), typos ('SMLP model', 'datset', 'differnet', 'In a addition', 'harness the performance' where 'hamper' is meant), and Eq. 9 notation overloads R for both camera rotation and rasterization.
The claimed ability to recover high-frame-rate sharp video from sub-frame motion is asserted but never evaluated quantitatively.

strengths: The paper addresses a clearly motivated and previously unexplored problem: reconstructing sharp, animatable 3DGS human avatars directly from motion-blurred multi-view video. The claim of being the first method for this task appears credible based on the related work survey.

The technical formulation is sound: extending the 2D physical blur integration model (Eq. 1-2) to a 3D-aware formulation (Eq. 3) built on SMPL-driven warping of canonical 3D Gaussians is a natural but well-executed generalization, and the decomposition into sub-frame motion modeling plus canonical sharp avatar optimization is a sensible way to handle the ill-posedness.

The B-spline (De Boor-Cox) sub-frame pose interpolation with a learned pose-displacement CNN, together with the inter-frame Geodesic-distance regularization (Eq. 9), directly targets the directional ambiguity illustrated in Fig. 1, and the ablation in Tab. 4/Fig. 8 provides concrete evidence that this regularization specifically fixes non-midpoint timestep errors (e.g., PSNR at non-middle timesteps rises from 24.42 to 25.42 for Kblur=5).

The paper establishes a new benchmark for this task: a synthetic dataset derived from ZJU-MoCap with RIFE-interpolated blur synthesis, and a real-world dataset captured with a purpose-built 360-degree hybrid-exposure camera system (4 blurry + 8 sharp synchronized views, documented hardware and timing in Tab. 1 and Fig. 5). This is a significant community contribution, with a stated commitment to release code and data.

The evaluation is unusually thorough: comparisons against five two-stage deblurring baselines (Tab. 2), ablations over trajectory representations (Tab. 5), knot count P (Tab. 6), virtual image count T (Tab. 7), blur magnitudes Kblur (Tab. 10-11), training view counts (Tab. 13-14), SMPL initialization perturbations (Tab. 8), mask quality (Tab. 12), novel-pose animation (Fig. 13), and a monocular iPhone demo (Fig. 14). The improvements over baselines are large and consistent (e.g., ~2.5 dB PSNR and ~0.08 LPIPS on synthetic data).

Limitations are candidly and specifically discussed (linear-radiance vs. sRGB averaging, SMPL's inability to model handheld objects/loose garments, 3DGS geometry fidelity), which reflects scientific maturity.
weaknesses: The baseline comparison set is narrow. All quantitative comparisons reduce to '2D deblurring + GauHuman'. Existing blur-aware 3D reconstruction methods cited in the paper (e.g., Bad-Gaussians, DyBluRF, BARF-style deblurring) are dismissed collectively but not empirically compared, even in adapted form; this leaves the superiority claim relative to the closest 3D deblurring methodology unverified, even if those methods are not natively animatable.

The method is essentially GauHuman plus added blur-aware machinery (interpolation, pose deformation CNN, LBS offset CNN, shape optimization). Some ablation components contribute marginally: shape optimization adds only ~0.02 dB PSNR on synthetic data and ~0.05 dB on real data (Tab. 3), and B-spline vs. Slerp differs by ~0.03 dB (Tab. 5), so the individual contributions of several modules are close to noise level; only 'w/o interp.' and 'w/o pose deform' show meaningful drops.

The synthetic blur model has simplifications that weaken the claimed realism: blur is synthesized by averaging RIFE-interpolated frames, and the paper itself acknowledges (Sec. 4.5.2) that averaging non-linear sRGB values is physically inaccurate. Additionally, the synthetic GT sharp frames for intermediate timesteps come from interpolation rather than capture, which may advantage the proposed blur-synthesis-matching loss.

The real dataset is small (8 scenes, 12 cameras, 4 blurry training views) and uses fixed train/test view splits; quantitative evaluation on real data is limited to novel-view sharp frames, and the Lreg ablation cannot be quantitatively evaluated on real data due to lack of GT for non-middle timesteps (Sec. 4.3), leaving part of the core claim (inter-frame direction disambiguation) supported only by synthetic results.

Several presentation issues reduce polish: a grammatical error in Sec. 4.2 ('inconsist 2D deblurring'), Table 5 is labeled 'Qualitative ablation results' but contains quantitative metrics, and the loss description references Sec. 3.2 for Lreg although it is defined under the optimization section; Eq. 6's De Boor-Cox matrix is stated without derivation or validation of its correctness.

Training/inference cost relative to GauHuman is not reported. Rendering T=5 virtual sharp images per blurry frame per iteration and optimizing per-joint control knots presumably increases training time substantially; the practical trade-off is unclear.

The two-stage baseline evaluation protocol could be better justified: the 2D deblurring models were presumably trained on general blur data and applied zero-shot to this domain, so their poor multi-view consistency claim, while plausible, is supported mainly by the modest gap between direct-3DGS and 2D-deblur+3DGS rows rather than by a stronger 3D-consistent restoration baseline.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem setting: the paper appears to be the first to address reconstruction of sharp, animatable 3D Gaussian avatars directly from blurry multi-view videos, and the ambiguity analysis in Fig. 1 (static vs. unordered vs. ordered sharp interpretations of a blur) clearly motivates why existing avatar pipelines and two-stage 2D deblurring + avatar baselines are insufficient.

The proposed 3D-aware blur formation model (Eq. 3) is a natural and technically sensible extension of 2D blur formation: averaging rasterizations of a canonical 3DGS avatar warped by sub-frame SMPL parameters, with B-spline pose interpolation plus a learned pose displacement to capture non-rigid sub-frame motion.

Significant community contribution through data: a synthetic blurred benchmark built from ZJU-MoCap with RIFE-interpolated frame averaging, and a real 360-degree hybrid-exposure capture rig (4 blurry cameras with 50 ms exposure and ND filter + 8 sharp cameras, time-synchronized) that enables genuine real-world evaluation with sharp ground truth for novel views. Code and data are promised for release.

Large and consistent quantitative margins over baselines: ~25.5 vs. ~23.1 dB PSNR on the synthetic set and ~27.0 vs. ~25.6 dB on the real set (Tab. 2), maintained across blur magnitudes Kblur = 7/9/11 (Tab. 10) and reduced training views Nview = 2/3/4 (Tab. 13).

Unusually thorough ablation and robustness analysis: component ablations, trajectory representations (linear/slerp/B-spline), control knot count P, virtual image count T, inter-frame regularization evaluated separately at middle vs. non-middle timesteps (Tab. 4), SMPL initialization perturbations (Tab. 8), mask estimation robustness (Tab. 12), and a monocular iPhone demo with TRAM-estimated SMPL.

The ablation of Lreg (Tab. 4) honestly reports a small trade-off at the middle timestep (25.567 -> 25.546 PSNR) in exchange for substantially better non-middle timesteps (24.421 -> 25.417), which supports the claim that the regularization resolves motion-direction ambiguity rather than merely boosting headline metrics.
The limitations section is candid and specific (sRGB vs. linear-space averaging, geometry/BRDF, SMPL's inability to model handheld objects and loose garments).
weaknesses: The baseline comparison does not include adaptations of existing blur-aware 3D reconstruction methods (e.g., BAD-Gaussians [85], BARD-GS [43], DyBluRF [64], Deblur-NeRF [44]) to the avatar setting. The paper cites these as related work for dynamic-scene deblurring, and even a best-effort adaptation or a clear explanation of why they are inapplicable would substantially strengthen the 'first' and 'superior' claims. As presented, the main comparison is against 2D deblurring front-ends, which are known to lack multi-view consistency, making the large margin somewhat expected.

The evaluation protocol has gaps: quantitative results for non-middle timesteps on real data are excluded 'due to the lack of GT frames' (Tab. 4), so the key directional-ambiguity argument for Lreg is only validated on synthetic data where the blur was generated by frame averaging. Similarly, the real dataset cannot directly verify the synthetic blur model's fidelity.

The synthetic benchmark itself is quite idealized: blur generated by averaging RIFE-interpolated frames from ZJU-MoCap, with 'ideal' masks available. Although Tab. 12 shows robustness to SAM/rembg masks, the synthetic setting does not include sensor-level effects (noise, ISP, rolling-shutter-like artifacts) that the authors themselves acknowledge in the limitations.

No efficiency analysis is reported. Rendering T=5 virtual sharp images per blurry frame per iteration, plus CNN-based pose displacement and LBS-offset prediction, presumably costs substantially more than GauHuman; training time and inference/rendering speed relative to baselines should be reported, especially since speed is a key selling point of 3DGS-based avatars.

Several component ablations show small margins (e.g., full model vs. w/o shape opt.: 25.546 vs. 25.529 PSNR; B-spline vs. Slerp: 25.546 vs. 25.539), and no variance/statistical significance is reported, making it hard to judge which components are genuinely material versus noise. The dominant factor is clearly the interpolation scheme (w/o interp. drops ~1.5 dB).

Quantitative evaluation relies mainly on novel-view PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS of the rendered avatar; no pose or motion accuracy metrics are reported despite the paper's emphasis on recovering correct sub-frame motion, and novel-pose animation quality (Fig. 13) is only qualitative.

Presentation issues: minor but recurring typographical and grammatical errors (e.g., 'decribed' in Sec. 3.3, 'inconsist 2D deblurring' in Sec. 4.2, 'Tab. 4 proves'/'results in Tab. 9 proofs' in Sec. 4.4), and Table 1 reports 'Scene number 8' with 'Picture format PNG' in a configuration table, which reads awkwardly.

The multi-view setting (4 calibrated static blurry cameras plus 8 sharp test cameras) is a relatively controlled capture scenario; the leap to practical monocular or unconstrained settings is only demonstrated qualitatively on a single iPhone capture without quantitative support.

strengths: Addresses a clearly motivated and previously unaddressed problem: reconstructing sharp, animatable 3D Gaussian avatars directly from blurry video, whereas prior avatar methods require sharp inputs and prior blur-aware NeRF/GS methods are not animatable.

The 3D-aware blur formation model (Eq. 3) is a sensible and well-grounded extension of the standard 2D blur integration to the avatar setting, and decomposing the ill-posed problem into sub-frame motion estimation plus canonical 3DGS optimization is a clean formulation.

The B-spline based sub-frame pose model with a CNN pose-displacement correction, plus the inter-frame Geodesic regularization (Eq. 9), directly targets the motion ambiguities illustrated in Fig. 1, and the ablations (Tables 3-5, Fig. 8) support the contribution of each component.

Significant experimental effort: a synthetic benchmark derived from ZJU-MoCap and a purpose-built real-world 360-degree hybrid-exposure capture system (blurry and sharp cameras synchronized, ND-filtered for consistent intensity), enabling both quantitative and novel-view evaluation that did not previously exist for this task.

Large quantitative improvements over all baselines (e.g., synthetic PSNR 25.55 vs ~23.1; LPIPS 0.148 vs ~0.22), with consistent gains across blur magnitudes (Table 10), varying view counts (Table 13), mask estimators (Table 12), and SMPL perturbations (Table 8), plus novel-pose animation and a monocular iPhone demo demonstrating generality.
Honest limitations section discussing linear-vs-sRGB averaging, geometry/BRDF recovery, and SMPL's inability to model loose garments or handheld objects.
weaknesses: Baselines are limited: comparisons are only GauHuman trained on blurry frames, or GauHuman trained after generic 2D video deblurring (RVRT/VRT/ShiftNet/BSST). The paper does not adapt or compare against existing blur-aware radiance field methods (e.g., BAD-Gaussians/BAD-NeRF style approaches) with SMPL-based motion, which would more directly test whether the specific 3D human motion model, rather than simply any blur-aware optimization, is the key factor.

The real dataset is modest in scale (8 scenes, 4 blurry training cameras, 8 sharp test cameras), and the real-data evaluation protocol (metrics computed on the 8 sharp-view cameras while trained on blurry ones) is reasonable but the calibration dependency on EasyMoCap run on blurry input could confound comparisons with the two-stage baselines; this is not analyzed.

Some design choices and components are under-specified for reproducibility: architecture and training details of the pose-displacement CNN and LBS-offset CNN are minimal, and the real-data gain over the best two-stage baseline is comparatively small on PSNR/SSIM (e.g., 27.01 vs 25.57-25.57 PSNR, but SSIM differences of ~0.02), so the real-data improvement rests largely on LPIPS.

The synthetic blur is generated by averaging RIFE-interpolated frames from only Kblur sharp frames, which is an approximation of true exposure integration; robustness to more realistic blur (e.g., with noise, ISP effects) is not evaluated, and the authors themselves note the sRGB-averaging discrepancy only as future work.

The 'first model for reconstructing sharp animatable avatars from blurry video' claim should be stated more carefully relative to concurrent blur-aware dynamic GS work (e.g., [43]); the distinction (animatable avatar vs. dynamic scene) is valid but deserves explicit discussion.

Small inconsistencies and typos (e.g., 'inconsist 2D deblurring', decribed, 'deform' vs 'deform' naming in Table 3/Fig. 7, Table 5 labeled 'Qualitative' though quantitative) slightly detract from polish.
